metadata.agenda_item: 17D. INITIATION OF AN AMENDMENT TO THE ZONING CODE, ZONING MAP AND GENERAL PLAN AND LAND USE MAP TO IDENTIFY APPROPRIATE LOCATIONS FOR TRUCK INTENSIVE INDUSTRIAL USES AND PROVIDE REASONABLE DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS TO PROTECT NEIGHBORING RESIDENTIAL NEIGHBORHOODS FROM THE IMPACTS OF EXCESSIVE TRUCK TRAFFIC
metadata.note: Machine transcript; timestamps are relative to audio clip start.

segments.text: Okay, moving on to item D, initiation of an amendment to the zoning code, zoning map and
general plan and land use map to identify appropriate locations for truck intensive
industrial uses and provide reasonable development standards to protect neighboring residential
neighborhoods from the impacts of excessive truck traffic.
Mr. Fresk, can I have the staff report on this item?
Yes, thank you Madam Mayor and Council members as the Council's aware we've had several land
use entitlement applications that have come before the city that actually are truck intensive.
They require a lot of vehicle trips with trucks and I believe we're all aware of the
impacts that truck traffic has, it has an impact on traffic congestion, it has an impact
on air pollution, it has an impact on our infrastructure and oftentimes these impacts
have a disproportionate effect on our residents, particularly residential communities.
When we talk about truck intensive uses, we've identified some of those in the staff report,
I'll mention them just for the, particularly for the benefit of the public.
But we're looking at truck and transport uses, truck and semi-trailer storage yards,
heavy equipment, sales and rental, auto auction, salvage yards, contractor storage yards,
and another use is warehouse and distribution centers as well.
And there are three different areas that have, that we've identified that really could benefit
from clarity if we go back and analyze the main land use documents that we use to,
when we're reviewing entitlements, our zoning ordinance, our general plan land use map,
and our design guidelines.
So we've identified some areas that really need clarification as well as the need to
really go back and look comprehensively at the city and identify what areas make sense
for these types of uses and what areas don't.
And what design standards can we, can we apply that really, again, at clarity, not only for
staff in applying the city's, the city council's vision toward these types of uses, but also
for the development community.
So they're clear when they look at our code, they have a clear understanding of where these
types of uses can go.
This evening, what we're recommending is that the city council initiate an effort for us
to conduct a study and look at all of those documents that I just mentioned to those land
use documents and to do so in a way that really addresses the concerns that have been expressed
by the council.
I think there's, there is an understanding that this type of, these types of uses and
the truck uses that are generated from this do have an impact, a negative impact on the
public's health, safety and welfare.
And so, so we are looking for a direction to do that as far as that initiation process.
And of course, that process would come back through after our analysis to the planning commission
for review and recommendation, and then back again to the city council.
In addition to that analysis and that initiation, we're also recommending the adoption of an
urgency ordinance that would apply a moratorium on those types of uses.
It would basically put a pause on those types of uses right now while we conduct this analysis.
And then once we do that, we bring it back up to the city council.
We make the council that makes whatever changes are appropriate.
The moratorium would then be lifted.
And we would then apply those new standards to any applications.
I would like to make mention to you that of all those different uses that I identified
on that list, I do want to call out the issue of warehouse and distribution centers because
that's an important distinction here.
The moratorium really doesn't address warehouse and distribution centers.
And the reason why that is, is because there's two areas that are specified in the city where
you can have those types of uses.
It's the Miraloma Overlay Zone and the Algomonta.
So outside of that, no one can come in and do distribution of warehousing.
So we felt that the code already addresses that.
But the draft urgency ordinance that is presented before you this evening does give the city
council flexibility if you want to modify those overlay zones.
So if there's a project that for whatever reason has a tremendous community benefit is located
in an area that the council seems appropriate, the council has the ability to still approve
that type of project.
So you're not handcuffed or limited by that moratorium in that way.
So if the council does adopt an urgency ordinance, it would require a four fifth vote to do that.
It is good for 45 days, which means that because our study would take much longer than that,
we're probably looking at approximately a year to do that.
We would bring back to you, most likely in February, a request to extend that moratorium.
And there's the ability to extend that twice.
So that essentially concludes my presentation.
We have received, again, letters regarding this particular item.
We've received approximately 10 letters from the community in support of this action,
including the moratorium.
We've also received one letter from Jonathan Chardlow.
He is representing a property where there's currently an auto auction, it's insurance auto auction,
which is located on Pyrite north of the 60 there, they're asserting and requesting that
because they are in the entitlement process that they be exempted from the moratorium.
So that's their request, as well as requesting a community workshop to be held.
And then there's one letter that was submitted by Robert Evans, he's the executive director
of the National Association of Industrial and Office Properties.
And it's a letter of opposition, particularly for the moratorium.
And all of those letters have been provided to the city council for your review.
And that concludes my presentation.
I'm, of course, available for any questions you might have.
Thank you.
Thank you, Mr. President.
Any questions for staff?
I would.
Okay.
During the pause, what happens to pretty much all the situation?
That's a very good question.
So if an application has already been submitted prior to the, prior to the initiation, the
moratorium, I should say, prior to the application of that.
One thing on those types of applications, they cannot receive approval.
So they can't go to the planning commission for action or the city council.

So if they can, they can just sit and pause and not move any further, or they can continue
to move through the process, we can continue to evaluate it and so forth at their costs
and at their risk.
But there would be no assurance at the end of the day that they could even receive approval
because the standards and the requirements may change.
So that's why we say it's at a certain risk and at their risk.
So that's sort of what happens now for folks who want to come in and apply after the moratorium,
we won't accept that application for these types of uses.
And assuming they're, I don't think they would be operating at the moment, so it wouldn't
apply that.

I'm writing to express my support for imposing a moratorium on the expansion of truck intensive

We urge the Council to approve the moratorium to study the impacts and move towards a green
and just economy.

This temporary moratorium will allow city agencies to come up with a solution that would
be in the best interest of the community.

I was so pleased to see this item on the agenda, the constant pressure in our city to turn valuable
